title: Claisen–Schmidt condensation
subtitle: Acetone and benzaldehyde: aldol, then E1cB to benzalacetone

reactants.caption: acetone + benzaldehyde + sodium hydroxide
reactants.learnerPrompt: Two carbonyl compounds and a base. Which one can form an enolate? Form it.
hintTiers: Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogens, so it cannot form an enolate. Acetone can.
Hydroxide takes one of the drawn hydrogens of acetone; the C–H electrons form a C=C bond; the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → a drawn α-hydrogen of acetone; that C–H bond → a π bond to the carbonyl carbon; the C=O π bond → a lone pair on the acetone oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide can add to benzaldehyde, but the hydrate is a reversible dead end. Use hydroxide as a base on acetone.
Hydroxide can add to acetone's C=O, but that is reversible and leads nowhere. Hydroxide is the base here.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the proton is taken and a C=C forms. The carbonyl carbon now has five bonds: move the C=O π electrons onto oxygen.

enolate.caption: acetone enolate + water + benzaldehyde
hintTiers: The enolate's α-carbon is the nucleophile. Which carbon of benzaldehyde is electrophilic?
The oxygen lone pair re-forms C=O, the C=C π electrons form a bond to the aldehyde carbon, and the aldehyde C=O π electrons move onto its oxygen. Three arrows.
Enolate oxygen lone pair → a π bond to its carbon; the C=C π bond → a new bond from the CH₂ carbon to the aldehyde carbon; the aldehyde C=O π bond → a lone pair on the aldehyde oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Attack through oxygen is possible but reversible and gives nothing useful. The aldol needs the new C–C bond: the C=C π bond attacks.
The carbonyl oxygen is electron-rich. The electrophile is the aldehyde carbon.
Taking the proton back from water just gives acetone again. Let the enolate attack benzaldehyde.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right bonds, but this leaves a cation next to O⁻ on the acetone side. Push the enolate oxygen lone pair in too.

alkoxide.caption: the alkoxide + water
hintTiers: An alkoxide is a strong base. Which proton source is nearby?
The alkoxide takes a proton from water. Two arrows.
Alkoxide lone pair → the drawn hydrogen of water; that O–H bond → a lone pair on the water oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking the new C–C bond is the retro-aldol, the reverse step. Protonate the alkoxide instead.
Both oxygens are electron-rich. The alkoxide takes the δ+ hydrogen of water.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the alkoxide takes the proton. Now break the O–H bond onto the water oxygen.

aldol.caption: 4-hydroxy-4-phenylbutan-2-one (the aldol) + hydroxide
aldol.learnerPrompt: The aldol does not stop here. Hydroxide removes a proton again: form the new enolate.
hintTiers: The CH₂ between the C=O and the CH(OH) still has an acidic hydrogen. Why does deprotonating it lead somewhere new?
Hydroxide takes the drawn hydrogen on that CH₂; the C–H electrons form a C=C bond to the carbonyl carbon; the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → the drawn hydrogen on the CH₂; that C–H bond → a π bond to the carbonyl carbon; the C=O π bond → a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, so a concerted E2 is not possible. Form the enolate first: its electrons will push hydroxide out.
Hydroxide does not leave from a neutral molecule on its own. Make the enolate first.
Taking the proton off the OH group just goes back to the alkoxide. The productive proton is on the carbon next to the C=O.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the proton is taken and a C=C forms. Now move the C=O π electrons onto oxygen.

aldol-enolate.caption: the enolate of the aldol + water
hintTiers: Electrons from the enolate oxygen can flow along the C=C bond towards the carbon carrying the OH group.
The oxygen lone pair re-forms C=O, the C=C π bond moves one bond along, and the C–OH bond breaks onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Enolate oxygen lone pair → a π bond to its carbon; the C=C π bond → a π bond to the carbon carrying OH; the C–OH bond → a lone pair on that oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking the proton back just reverses the last step. Let the enolate push hydroxide out.
That would make a strained four-membered ring. The enolate's electrons flow along the C=C bond to push hydroxide out.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide does leave, but only because the enolate pushes it. Add the arrows from the enolate oxygen and the C=C bond.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Only acetone has α-hydrogens, so only one enolate can form. That is why this crossed aldol gives one main product.
The enolate adds to the aldehyde rather than to another acetone: an aldehyde is more electrophilic than a ketone, and benzaldehyde is present in excess over the enolate.
This is the aldol addition product, a β-hydroxy ketone. Hydroxide is given back.
The enolate of the aldol sits next to a carbon carrying a leaving group, which sets up E1cB.

E1cB: hydroxide is a poor leaving group, but the new C=C bond is conjugated with both the C=O group and the benzene ring, so dehydration is fast and complete. The E alkene forms, with the phenyl group and the carbonyl group apart.

mechanismSummary: Hydroxide deprotonates acetone, the only partner with α-hydrogens. The enolate adds to benzaldehyde, the better electrophile, and water protonates the alkoxide: the aldol. A second deprotonation gives an enolate that expels hydroxide by E1cB, giving (E)-benzalacetone, conjugated from the ring through the C=C to the C=O. A crossed aldol works cleanly when one partner cannot enolise and is the better electrophile.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 26
